intro: Fit a model to real-looking data the way a graphing calculator does: linear, quadratic, cubic, quartic, exponential, logarithmic or sinusoidal. The model is drawn through the points, each residual is a short line from the point to the model, and the residual plot sits underneath. Residuals that scatter with no pattern mean the model fits the shape of the data; a curve or a wave in them means another model will do better. Drag the prediction line to read the model's value to three decimal places.
howItWorks:
• Least squares. Each model's constants make the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible, the way the calculator's regressions do.
  • Residual = actual $y$ − predicted $y$. Above the model is positive, below is negative.
  • Exponential ($y = a \cdot b^x$) is fit as a line through $(x, \ln y)$, and logarithmic ($y = a + b\ln x$) as a line through $(\ln x, y)$, as ExpReg and LnReg do; so the data need $y > 0$ or $x > 0$.
  • Sinusoidal ($y = a\sin(bx + c) + d$): the frequency $b$ is found by search, then $a$, $c$ and $d$ by least squares. Use radians.
  • Three decimals. Constants are stored, not rounded: a prediction made from rounded constants can miss the third decimal. Round only the final answer.
  • Pattern test. The residual plot is read by a runs test on the signs of the residuals in order of $x$: long runs of one sign mean a pattern.
